G|D1.dim: how far the business looked for other work
G|D1.attr: When Ferncombe Bakery stopped making deliveries, it made a delivery driver redundant after asking its one manager whether there was other work the driver could do, but without looking further.

G|D2.dim: how far the appeal was heard apart from the decision
G|D2.attr: Ashgrove Dental dismissed a receptionist for repeatedly missing shifts. The receptionist appealed, and the appeal was heard by the person who had made the decision to dismiss, with a second manager sitting in, and was upheld.

draws.text:
# Answer: No

The appeal should have been conducted by someone other than the person who made the original dismissal decision to ensure impartiality and fairness. Having the original decision-maker conduct their own appeal hearing fails to meet the procedural standard required for fair dismissal.

No.

The appeal was heard by the person who made the original dismissal decision. Fair dismissal procedures require the appeal to be heard by someone independent and not involved in the original decision. This applies regardless of employer size.

No.

The appeal should have been heard by someone not involved in the original dismissal decision. Having the person who dismissed the receptionist conduct the appeal fails to meet the procedural fairness standard required, even for small employers.

No.

The appeal should have been heard by someone who was not involved in the original dismissal decision. According to the ACAS Code of Practice (which applies to this employer), an appeal must be conducted impartially by someone who has not previously been involved in the matter. Having the original decision-maker hear the appeal fails to meet this standard.

No.

The appeal was heard by the person who made the original dismissal decision. Best practice and fair procedure standards require that appeals should be heard by someone independent of the original decision. Having the original decision-maker hear the appeal compromises impartiality.

No.

The appeal should have been heard by someone who was not involved in the original dismissal decision. Having the person who dismissed the employee hear their own appeal fails the standard of impartiality required under UK employment law and the ACAS Code of Practice.

No.

The appeal was heard by the person who made the original dismissal decision, which violates the standard that appeals should be heard by someone independent of the original decision-maker. This procedural defect would typically render the dismissal procedurally unfair.

No.

The appeal was heard by the person who made the original dismissal decision. For employers with 20+ staff (Ashgrove has 2,000), the standard requires that an appeal should be heard by someone who was not involved in the original decision to ensure impartiality.

G|D3.dim: how far the one person's view was checked
G|D3.attr: Kilnworth Garage dismissed a mechanic for taking a customer's car out on a personal errand. The person who looked into what had happened also made the decision to dismiss, after a second manager had read the notes.

draws.text:
No.

Under UK employment law standards (the ACAS Code of Practice on Disciplinary Procedures), the employer should have conducted a disciplinary hearing where the mechanic was given an opportunity to respond to the allegations before dismissal. The question indicates investigation and managerial review occurred, but there is no mention of the employee being given the chance to present their case or defend themselves, which is a required procedural step.

No.

The dismissal procedure appears incomplete. Under UK employment law standards, a fair dismissal requires a proper disciplinary hearing where the employee has an opportunity to respond to allegations before dismissal is decided. The description shows an investigation and management review, but no mention of a formal hearing or the employee's right to respond.

G|D4.dim: how the earlier warnings were given
G|D4.attr: Marsh Lane Nurseries dismissed a gardener for using the company van for personal trips. The gardener had been warned twice before, once in writing and once by word of mouth, and was dismissed after the third occasion.

G|D5.dim: what the choice was based on
G|D5.attr: When orders fell, Harbour Print chose which machine operator to make redundant by the manager's reading of each operator's attendance record, without scoring the operators against any written criteria.

draws.text:
No.

A fair redundancy selection process requires objective, written criteria to be applied consistently and transparently. Subjective judgment based on reading attendance records without any written scoring system against predetermined criteria falls short of the legal standard for fair redundancy procedures.

G|D6.dim: how much warning of the meeting the assistant had
G|D6.attr: Tollgate Hardware dismissed a sales assistant for taking money from the till, after watching security footage. The assistant was told of the meeting the day before, and was told of the dismissal at the end of it.

draws.text:
No.

One day's notice of a disciplinary meeting is generally insufficient under UK employment law standards for fair dismissal procedures. Employees should typically be given reasonable notice (usually several days) to prepare their response and arrange representation, even in cases of serious misconduct.

G|K1.dim: how plainly and how often the warning came
G|K1.attr: Sam was copied into an email from a colleague saying, among other points, that a large borrower's loan had been graded using out-of-date accounts. Sam read the email and did nothing further. The borrower defaulted four months later, and the bank lost £2 million more than it would have done had the loan been graded on current accounts.

G|K2.dim: how long the report had shown the breach
G|K2.attr: The firm's monthly breach report, which Alex received, showed one fund over its limit on holdings in a single company for the first time that month. Alex took no step, and the breach went on for five more months until an auditor raised it.

G|K3.dim: how long the renewal sat unsigned
G|K3.attr: The contract with the supplier of the company's overnight payments system ran out, and the renewal had sat unsigned for a week on a shared list of tasks that Charlie read each week. The system failed for a day in June, and 40,000 customer payments were delayed.

G|K4.dim: how much was known of the risk when the plan was agreed
G|K4.attr: At a meeting Jamie attended, a plan to lend more to buy-to-let landlords was agreed after a short discussion, but no written analysis, of what would happen if rents fell, and Jamie raised no question about it. Rents fell the following year, and arrears on those loans tripled.

G|K5.dim: how much of the model was reviewed
G|K5.attr: A new pricing model went live after Emery had looked over its results and most of its assumptions, but not the one about the cost of claims. One assumption about the rising cost of claims was out of date, and home insurance premiums were set too low for a year, costing the insurer £5 million.

G|K6.attr: The quarterly complaints figures reached Finley and showed complaints about one savings account rising threefold in a year. Finley passed the figures on without comment, and the cause, interest paid at the wrong rate, went uncorrected for another eight months.

G|S1.dim: how much of the money went into the fund
G|S1.attr: Tarn Capital recommended putting a tenth of the money the client had to invest into a fund that trades currency options, without asking what experience the client had of such funds. The fund lost 40% in a year.

draws.text:
No.

Firms must ensure recommendations are suitable regardless of client categorization. Even when advising professional clients, recommending a high-risk, complex product (currency options) representing 10% of investment without assessing the client's actual knowledge and experience of such instruments fails to meet the suitability standard under MiFID II.

Yes.

The standard applicable to advising professional clients is lower. For professional clients, the firm is not required to conduct the same detailed fact-finding about experience with complex investments. The professional client classification itself means the firm can proceed without inquiring into the client's specific knowledge of such products.

No.

Even for professional clients, a firm must assess suitability and gather information about the client's knowledge, experience, and financial situation before making recommendations. Failing to ask about experience with currency options funds—a complex and volatile instrument—falls short of this standard.

G|S2.dim: what the firm sent about the bond
G|S2.attr: Brindle Partners recommended a bank bond that converts into shares if the bank gets into difficulty. It sent the bond's terms with a one-page guide to such bonds but did not check whether the client knew how such bonds work. The bank got into difficulty, the bond was converted, and the client lost 60% of the sum invested.

draws.text:
No.

A firm advising a retail client on a complex financial product (a contingent convertible bond) must assess the client's knowledge and understanding of such instruments before recommending them. Merely sending documentation without verifying the client's understanding falls short of the required suitability standard, particularly given the product's complexity and significant loss risk.

G|S3.dim: how far the firm tested understanding
G|S3.attr: Oxley Wealth recommended a product whose return depended on two stock market indices, asked the client one question about how it worked, and accepted a vague answer. The indices fell, and the product returned nothing for five years.

G|S4.dim: how long the fund was to be held
G|S4.attr: Halden Investments recommended holding, for a year, a fund that aims to return three times the daily movement of a share index. It sent the fund's documents but did not check whether the client knew how such funds behave over long periods. The index rose over three years, and the fund lost 20%.

draws.text:
No.

Even though professional clients receive less protection, the firm still has a duty to act honestly, fairly, and professionally. Recommending a leveraged fund designed for daily rebalancing to be held for a year, without verifying the client's understanding of how such funds deteriorate over longer periods due to volatility decay, falls short of this standard—particularly given the actual losses incurred despite positive index performance.

No.

The firm failed to meet the required standard by not assessing the client's knowledge and understanding of leveraged funds before recommending them. For retail clients, advisers must verify suitability, which includes checking whether clients understand complex investment products, particularly regarding their long-term behavior. The firm's failure to do so constitutes a breach of this obligation.

No.

For a retail client, Halden Investments must meet the **suitability standard** - ensuring recommendations are suitable for the client's knowledge, experience, and circumstances. By recommending a complex 3x leveraged fund without checking whether the client understood how such funds perform over longer periods (they decay due to volatility compounding), the firm failed to adequately assess suitability before giving advice. Merely sending documents is insufficient.

G|S5.dim: how much of the money went into the fund
G|S5.attr: Penrose Advisers recommended putting a tenth of the money into a property fund that can stop investors taking their money out, without asking what experience the client had of such funds. A year later the client asked to sell, and the fund had stopped withdrawals for nine months.

draws.text:
No.

The firm failed to meet the standard by recommending a fund with restricted liquidity (suspension of withdrawals) to a retail client without first assessing the client's experience, knowledge, and understanding of such funds. This violates the suitability requirements that apply to firms advising retail clients.

No.

A financial adviser must assess a client's knowledge and experience before recommending restricted/illiquid funds. Failing to do so before recommending a property fund with potential withdrawal restrictions breaches the suitability requirement that applies when advising retail clients.

G|S6.attr: Lowther Advisory recommended a bond issued by a small unlisted company, as one of five bonds, without asking whether the client had held such bonds before. The company failed two years later, and the bond was worth nothing.

draws.text:
Yes.

When advising a professional client, the firm is not required to gather detailed information about the client's prior experience with specific security types before making recommendations. Professional clients receive less stringent protection than retail clients, and recommending an unlisted bond as part of a diversified portfolio without prior questioning about such holdings would meet the applicable standard for professional client advice.

G|V1.dim: how far the details were checked on the call
G|V1.attr: The customer asked to set up a standing order. The call handler took the details, read them back once, set it up, and sent nothing in writing. The customer had given the wrong amount, and £900 instead of £90 left the account each month for three months.

G|V2.dim: how hard the only way to make the change was
G|V2.attr: The customer asked to move the date of a loan repayment. The call handler said this could only be done on a paper form sent by post, which took two days to arrive, and the next repayment was missed, adding a £12 fee.

draws.text:
No.

The firm should have made reasonable adjustments for a vulnerable customer who had already disclosed their health condition and need for accommodation on the call itself, rather than requiring them to undertake a cumbersome paper-based process that led to the missed payment.

G|V3.attr: The customer asked how to claim for a burst pipe. The call handler explained the claims process twice, did not offer to put it in writing, and ended the call. The customer missed the deadline for sending photographs, and the claim was delayed by a month.

draws.text:
No.

The firm failed to meet the required standard. When the customer disclosed they were hard of hearing, Sedgemoor Insurance should have offered to provide the claims process information in writing as a reasonable adjustment. Merely explaining twice verbally, without offering alternative formats, was insufficient given the customer's specific needs.

G|V4.dim: what the customer was told about the change
G|V4.attr: The customer asked to renew a car insurance policy. The call handler said that some terms had changed and were in the renewal letter, did not go through them, and renewed the policy. The new terms no longer covered driving abroad, and the customer had an accident in France the next month that was not covered.

G|V5.dim: how the call-back time was set
G|V5.attr: The customer asked to close a savings account. The call handler said a call back would be needed to finish the closure and booked one for 10am the next day without asking whether that time suited, and said it could be moved by phoning back. The customer missed the call, and the request lapsed.

G|V6.dim: how far the risk was gone through
G|V6.attr: The customer asked to move their pension savings into a different fund. The call handler read out the fund's risk description twice, made the switch on the call, and did not suggest waiting until someone could help. The new fund fell 15% over the following months.

G|W1.attr: A few everyday words in the essay were misspelt, among them 'becuase', 'beutiful' and 'thier'.

G|W2.attr: The essay was written as one long block with no paragraphs, and a few of its sentences ran into each other without full stops.

G|W3.dim: how many points had no support
G|W3.attr: The essay made four points about Roman roads but gave a reason for one of them and none for the other three.

G|W4.dim: how much of the essay was chatty
G|W4.attr: The essay was mostly formal, with a little slang such as 'gonna' and 'loads' and text abbreviations such as 'u' and 'b4'.

G|W5.dim: how often the point was repeated
G|W5.attr: The essay made the same point, that a good friend is kind, twice in slightly different words, and said little else.

G|W6.dim: how many stages were left out
G|W6.attr: The essay described rain falling and rivers running to the sea, but mentioned evaporation only in passing, so it never explained how the water gets back into the clouds.
